fields.title: Samuel Ajayi Crowther (For Teens)
fields.description: At about thirteen, Ajayi watched raiders burn his town, was led away with a rope around his neck, and was sold six times. A British warship freed him from a slave ship, and he grew up to give his people the Bible in their own language and to become the first African bishop of the Anglican Church. This teen edition tells the true story straight: the despair, the rescue, the mother found again, the shipwreck and the kidnapping, and the young missionaries who pulled his life’s work apart, and how he answered.
fields.hook: Captured at thirteen and sold six times. Freed from a slave ship. Became Africa’s first Anglican bishop.

qa.question: Who was Samuel Ajayi Crowther?
qa.answer: A Yoruba man from what is now south-western Nigeria, born about 1807. He was captured in a slave raid in 1821, freed from a slave ship by the Royal Navy in 1822, and became a teacher, a Niger explorer, the leading translator of the Yoruba Bible, and in 1864 the first African bishop of the Anglican Church.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It tells how, as a boy, he tried more than once to take his own life, and how he later confessed it. It also tells the story of his last years, when young European missionaries suspended his African clergy over his head, without pretending that his mission had no real problems.

qa.question: What does “Africa can chiefly be benefitted by her own Children” mean?
qa.answer: It is from a letter Crowther wrote in 1841, after a disastrous expedition in which many Europeans died of fever. He meant that Africans, who could live there and speak the languages, should be trained, trusted and sent to reach their own people with the gospel.

qa.question: Did he really meet Queen Victoria?
qa.answer: Yes, in 1851 at Windsor Castle. She came in quietly while he was showing Prince Albert some maps, lit the candles herself when the lamp went out, and heard him pray the Lord’s Prayer in Yoruba. She said it was “soft and melodious.”

qa.question: Was he removed as bishop?
qa.answer: No. In 1890 a committee at Onitsha suspended or dismissed some of his African clergy, including his own son. He withdrew from the committee in protest but remained bishop until he died. In 2014 the Archbishop of Canterbury said of how he was treated: “It was wrong.”

qa.question: How did he treat people of other religions?
qa.answer: With patience and respect. He believed Christ is the truth and said so plainly when asked, but he told his clergy not to dispute with Muslims or insult the worshippers of the old gods. He wanted them to show “sympathy with all classes of hearers.”

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length biography of Crowther, which draws on his own letters and journals and checks them against the missionary records and modern historians. A few stories were remembered by his family long afterwards, and this edition says so when it tells them.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from his story?
qa.answer: That God can be at work in the worst thing that ever happens to you without making it any less bad; that your own language and people are worth something to God; and that you can answer people who wrong you without becoming like them.

fields.title: The Unhappy, Blessed Day
fields.body_html:
“And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.” — Genesis 50:20 (ASV)

It was a fair morning in 1821 in Osogun, a Yoruba town of about twelve thousand people in what is now south-western Nigeria. A boy named Ajayi, about thirteen years old, was at home while his family got breakfast ready. Around nine o’clock a rumour ran through the town: the enemy was coming.

The Yoruba country was falling apart. Its old empire was splitting, and armed bands were roaming from town to town catching people to sell to the Portuguese and Spanish slave-buyers on the coast. Every town that fell meant more captives, and every sale meant more guns for the next raid. By the time anyone in Osogun could run, the raiders had surrounded it. After three or four hours of fighting, they were inside.

Ajayi described what came next years later, and it is one of the most vivid eyewitness accounts of a slave raid ever written. Mothers ran through thorn bushes with babies on their backs and children clinging to their arms, dropping their loads, then finding they could not save all their children either. Ajayi had a bow and five arrows. He lost the bow in the thorns before he could use it. The last time he saw his father was when his father came from the fighting to tell them to run. The raiders threw a noose of rope over the neck of every captive and led them off “in the manner of goats tied together.” Ajayi, his mother, his two sisters, one of them a baby, and a cousin were led out through the burning town. He caught sight of his grandmother in the crowd for a few minutes, and never saw her again.

Sixteen years later, now a Christian and a schoolmaster, he sat down to write about that day. He called it “the unhappy, but which I am now taught, in other respects, to call blessed day, which I shall never forget in my life.” Unhappy, because he was violently torn from his family. Blessed, because it was the first step of a journey that would bring him to Christ.

Read that carefully, because it is easy to get wrong. Crowther never said slavery was good. He never said his losses didn’t count. He ended his letter by saying the day was blessed “when considered in this respect; though certainly it must be unhappy also, in my being deprived on it of my father, mother, sisters, and all other relations.” He held on to both halves of that sentence for the rest of his life.

That is exactly how Joseph spoke in Genesis. His brothers sold him to slave-traders. Years later, when they were terrified he would take revenge, he did not tell them it had all been fine. He said, “ye meant evil against me.” It was evil. Then he said, “but God meant it for good.” God had been at work inside the evil, for purposes nobody could see at the time.

Maybe something has happened to you that was simply wrong: a loss, an injustice, something done to you. Christians sometimes rush to tell people that “everything happens for a reason,” as if the reason makes the wrong thing okay. Crowther and Joseph are more honest than that. You are allowed to call it unhappy. You are also allowed to hope that God is not finished with it.

One thing to do this week: think of the hardest thing that has happened to you. Write two sentences about it, starting the first with “It was unhappy because …” and the second with “God could still …” Don’t force the second one. If you can’t finish it yet, leave it blank and come back to it when you finish this book.

study_questions.question: What happened to Osogun in 1821?
study_questions.answer: Slave-raiders surrounded and broke into the town. Ajayi, his mother, his sisters and a cousin were captured and led away with ropes around their necks, and he never saw his father again.

study_questions.question: Why did Crowther call it both “unhappy” and “blessed”?
study_questions.answer: Unhappy because he lost his home and family; blessed because it began the journey that brought him to Christ. He never let the blessing cancel the grief.

study_questions.question: How is Joseph’s statement in Genesis 50:20 different from saying “everything happens for a reason”?
study_questions.answer: Joseph calls what his brothers did evil and does not excuse it. He says God was at work in it for good, which is not the same as saying the wrong thing was really fine.

fields.title: The Noose He Couldn’t Tighten
fields.body_html:
“And bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.” — Matthew 6:13 (ASV)

The day after the raid, the captives were brought to the raiders’ chief “as trophies at his feet.” Within twenty-four hours Ajayi was the property of three different people. He was traded for a horse, sent back when the horse turned out to be no good, and for three months was allowed to visit his mother, who was a captive in the same town. Then one evening he was sent on an errand and found himself chained up for market. At first light the traders marched out. Another boy in the chain begged to see his mother and was beaten into silence. Ajayi thought they walked past the very house where his own mother was. He did not dare say a word.

He was sold to a woman who took him south towards the coast. She talked cheerfully about going to the Popo country to buy tobacco. Ajayi knew what that meant: it was where the Portuguese bought slaves. He stopped eating. He got sick.

Then he decided to die. He wrote about it later with an honesty that still stops people:

“I determined with myself that I would not go to the Popo country; but would make an end of myself, one way or another. In several nights I attempted strangling myself with my band; but had not courage enough to close the noose tight, so as to effect my purpose. May the Lord forgive me this sin!”

He planned to jump out of the canoe at the next river. Before he could, his owner sold him on. At the next town he tried again, several times, and failed. He was traded for tobacco and rum, kept chained alone, and finally brought to a great lagoon. He had never seen so much water, and it terrified him. He was taken across it at night to Lagos, the slave port.

Here is the sentence he wrote about those months, sixteen years later: “Thus the Lord, while I knew Him not, led me not into temptation, and delivered me from evil.” He was quoting the Lord’s Prayer, a prayer he had never heard at the time. Looking back, he could see that it had been answered for him before he ever prayed it.

This is a heavy chapter, so let’s be direct. If you have ever felt the way that boy felt, that the only way out of the pain was to end your life, you are not the first, and you are not beyond God’s reach. Ajayi felt that way at thirteen. He went on to live about seventy more years, find his mother again, and help thousands of people find God. The despair was real. It was not the end of his story, and it does not have to be the end of yours.

And notice what he did with it. He didn’t hide it. He wrote it down, asked forgiveness, and told it so that others would know where God had found him. Darkness that gets named and brought into the light loses some of its power.

One thing to do this week: if you are carrying thoughts of hurting yourself, tell one safe person this week: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live. That is not weakness; it is exactly the kind of help God sends. If you’re not there, pray the line “deliver us from evil” slowly every day this week, for yourself and for someone you know who is struggling.

study_questions.question: What did he mean by saying the Lord “delivered me from evil” while he “knew Him not”?
study_questions.answer: That God had been protecting him through those months before he had ever heard of Christ or prayed the Lord’s Prayer.

study_questions.answer: Naming it and bringing it into the light let others see where God had found him, and showed that despair does not have to be the end of the story.

fields.title: Hogs and Cannon-Shot
fields.body_html:
“The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is upon me; because Jehovah hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the broken-hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound” — Isaiah 61:1 (ASV)

In Lagos, Ajayi was bought by Portuguese slave-traders, “the eighth in number.” By then, he said, he had become “a veteran in slavery” and “patiently took whatever came.” The captives were kept in a room with one door and no windows, the men and boys chained together by the neck. When the men pulled the chain tight to lie down, the boys’ necks were bruised. They lived like that for nearly four months.

Then, at night, they were taken out to a ship: 187 people. The crew didn’t feed them that first day, and most were seasick. “On the very same evening,” Crowther wrote, “we were surprised by two English men-of-war.” It was 7 April 1822. The warships were HMS Myrmidon and HMS Iphigenia of the Royal Navy’s anti-slavery squadron, which patrolled the West African coast to stop ships like this one.

Ajayi and five friends were rowed over to the Myrmidon. There they saw meat with white skin hanging up, which they had never seen on a pig, and rows of iron cannonballs on the deck. They worked it out: the white men had eaten the other captives, and those were their heads. Then “a close examination of the flesh with cloven foot, which resembled that of a hog,” and “a cautious approach to the shot,” showed them the truth: it was pork, and the balls were iron. Crowther told that story against himself for the rest of his life. It is funny, and it is also not foolish: the people the white men bought had never come back.

Within days the boys were “quite at home in the man-of-war.” The sailors gave them clothes. Then the Portuguese owner was brought on board in chains. Ajayi walked up to the man while he was being shaved and hit him on the head. He recorded it honestly, and judged it just as honestly: “an act, however, very wicked and unkind in its nature.”

That is worth stopping on. Who could blame him? But years later, as a Christian, he didn’t defend it as justice. He called it wicked. Revenge feels like freedom for about four seconds. Crowther learned that real freedom is something else.

On 17 June 1822 the Myrmidon landed its rescued captives at Sierra Leone, a British colony for people freed from slave ships. Ajayi was sent to a hill village called Bathurst. People told the new arrivals that they were free, “and we very soon believed them.”

When Jesus began his ministry, he stood up in the synagogue and read the verse at the top of this chapter: he had come “to proclaim release to the captives.” The captain of the Myrmidon didn’t know he was freeing a future bishop; he was doing his job. But that bruised boy would spend the rest of his life proclaiming a deeper release, from a deeper slavery, to his own people.

One thing to do this week: notice one moment this week when you want payback, even a small one: a comeback, a cold shoulder, a screenshot. Don’t act on it. Instead, ask yourself honestly what Crowther asked himself: is this justice, or is it just me wanting to hit back?

study_questions.question: Who rescued Ajayi, and when?
study_questions.answer: Two Royal Navy warships, HMS Myrmidon and HMS Iphigenia, stopped the Portuguese slave ship on 7 April 1822, the same evening it sailed.

study_questions.question: How did Crowther later judge his blow to the Portuguese owner?

fields.title: Same Boy, New Name
fields.body_html:
“Wherefore if any man is in Christ, he is a new creature: the old things are passed away; behold, they are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (ASV)

At Bathurst, Ajayi lived in the house of the missionary, Mr. Davey, and his wife, and went to the village school. He learned fast. “In about six months after my arrival at Sierra Leone,” he wrote, “I was able to read the New Testament with some degree of freedom; and was made a Monitor, for which I was rewarded with sevenpence-halfpenny per month.” A monitor taught the younger pupils. It was the first sign of what he would do all his life: learn something, then pass it on.

His conversion he described in one plain sentence: “The Lord was pleased to open my heart to hearken to those things which were spoken by His servants; and being convinced that I was a sinner, and desired to obtain pardon through Jesus Christ, I was baptized on the 11th of December 1825.” No vision, no lightning. He heard, he saw his need, and he wanted what Christ offered. And he gave God the credit even for the hearing.

At baptism he took a new name: Samuel Crowther, after a London vicar who had helped found the missionary society. Mrs. Davey had taught in that vicar’s Sunday school, and she chose the name. But here is the thing. He never stopped being Ajayi. For the rest of his life he signed himself Samuel Ajayi Crowther, using the old spelling Adjai. He spent decades studying the Yoruba language, proverbs and customs, and insisting the gospel should come to his people in their own tongue. What passed away was the slavery. What was made new was Ajayi.

In 1827 he became the very first student at a new college at Fourah Bay. He arrived with a mattress someone in England had given him on a short visit there. The principal, a strict German missionary named Haensel, banned it as “too great a luxury,” and made the students wash their own clothes and carry rice on their heads. Haensel worried that trips to England made Africans proud, which says more about Haensel than about Crowther. Crowther took the mattress away without complaint, and later spoke of Haensel with admiration.

His family remembered a story he loved to act out for his children. As a student monitor he was given heavy army boots to wear to church. He had never worn shoes. He couldn’t take a step. So he knelt in a corner, stood up holding the wall, and walked round and round the room until he could let go. For months he walked to church barefoot carrying the boots, and put them on at the door.

There was also a girl at Bathurst named Asano, baptised Susan Thompson, freed from a different slave ship six months after him. (Some retellings say they met on the slave ship. They didn’t.) In 1829 they married. It lasted fifty-one years.

Becoming a Christian does not mean becoming someone else. Some people think following Jesus means swapping their culture, personality or language for a churchier version. Paul says you are a “new creature,” not a different creature. God doesn’t erase the person he made. He frees them.

One thing to do this week: make a short list of three things about you that come from your family, culture or language: a food, a phrase, a tradition. For each one, ask: is this something Jesus wants to free me from, or something he wants to make new and use? Most things will be the second.

study_questions.question: How did Crowther describe his conversion?
study_questions.answer: Simply: the Lord opened his heart to listen, he became convinced he was a sinner, and he wanted forgiveness through Jesus Christ. He was baptised on 11 December 1825.

study_questions.question: Did taking the name Samuel Crowther mean he stopped being Ajayi?
study_questions.answer: No. He kept signing himself Samuel Ajayi Crowther and spent his life working in the Yoruba language and culture. His new life in Christ did not erase who he was.

study_questions.question: What is one part of your own background that God might want to use rather than erase?
study_questions.answer: Answers will vary. The chapter’s point is that being a “new creature” in Christ frees and renews the person God made rather than replacing them.

fields.title: Africa’s Own Children
fields.body_html:
“But ye shall receive power, when the Holy Spirit is come upon you: and ye shall be my witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judæa and Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.” — Acts 1:8 (ASV)

For twelve years Crowther was a schoolmaster and tutor in Sierra Leone. Then, in 1841, the British government sent three iron steamers up the Niger River to make treaties against the slave trade, start a model farm, and bring the gospel. The missionary society sent two missionaries with them. One was “Mr. Samuel Crowther.” He was in his early thirties, with a wife expecting another child and four children at home. His prayer as he left: “May the Lord, who has been my guide from my youth up until now, keep them and me.”

On the river he taught sailors the alphabet, led prayers, and worked on a Yoruba vocabulary. At one town he met Yoruba people for the first time in twenty years and heard what had happened to his homeland in the wars. Some Muslim traders there told him God approved of the slave trade. He let the argument go and simply told them that the God who had brought him so far could do greater things. When he described how freed Africans lived in Sierra Leone, people said they could judge how good it was “merely by my appearance.” Without trying, he was the expedition’s best argument.

Then the fever came. Almost every European fell ill. Men jumped overboard in delirium. The captain of Crowther’s ship, a godly man who had invited him to his Bible class, died. Of about 150 Europeans, 42 died within about two months. The model farm was abandoned. The society itself called the expedition an “admitted failure.” But most of the Africans had stayed well.

On 2 November 1841 Crowther wrote a letter to London. He was careful. He did not want to say Europeans were not needed. He even wrote that he and his fellow Africans were “not sufficiently qualified for so great a work.” But he said it anyway: “I am reluctantly led to adopt the opinion, that Africa can chiefly be benefitted by her own Children.”

That sentence became the idea of his whole life. Not that Africans were better than Europeans, but that Africans could live where Europeans died, already spoke the languages, and could go where others couldn’t. The question was whether the church would train them, trust them and send them. A German missionary on the expedition wrote home asking whether Crowther himself might be ordained and sent. Within two years, he was.

Look at the order in Acts 1:8: Jerusalem first, then Judea, then Samaria, then the ends of the earth. The witness starts at home and spreads out, carried by people in their own place. You are somebody’s “own.” There are people in your school, your family, your street and your language that you can reach more naturally than any missionary from outside.

Crowther did not wait until he felt qualified. He said plainly that he wasn’t. He went anyway, and he trusted that “human learning will be of very little avail, if the heart is not inspired by the Holy Spirit from above.”

One thing to do this week: write down the names of three people who are “your own”: same school, same team, same family, same language. Pick one and pray for them by name every day this week. If a natural moment comes to talk about what you believe, don’t dodge it.

study_questions.question: What did Crowther mean by “Africa can chiefly be benefitted by her own Children”?
study_questions.answer: That Africans, who could survive there and already spoke the languages, should be trained, trusted and sent to reach their own people, not that Europeans were unnecessary.

study_questions.question: Who are the “Jerusalem” people in your own life, the ones you can reach most naturally?
study_questions.answer: Answers will vary: family, classmates, teammates, neighbours. Acts 1:8 begins the witness at home, with the people closest to us.

fields.title: Who Makes You Different?
fields.body_html:
“For who maketh thee to differ? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? but if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory as if thou hadst not received it?” — 1 Corinthians 4:7 (ASV)

In 1842 Crowther sailed to England with a handwritten Yoruba grammar and vocabulary in his luggage. In 1843 the Bishop of London ordained him. The bishop said afterwards that his exam papers were “capital, and his Latin remarkably good.” (He was not, by the way, the first African ever ordained in the Church of England. Philip Quaque of Cape Coast was ordained in 1765. Crowther knew it; he had copied Quaque’s memorial with his own hand.)

He landed back in Freetown on 2 December 1843 and preached the next morning to a packed church. Lots of people had never seen an African clergyman. He wrote: “The novelty of seeing a native clergyman performing Divine Service excited a very great interest among all who were present. But the question, ‘Who maketh thee to differ?’ filled me with shame and confusion of face.”

Twenty-one years earlier he had been chained by the neck in a Lagos slave pen. Everything that now made him stand out, the education, the ordination, the pulpit, had been given to him. So what was there to boast about? That question, from the verse above, became the root of his humility for the rest of his life.

A few weeks later he did something that had probably never been done: he held a church service in Yoruba. He went house to house inviting people, even calling on the leader of the local Yoruba Muslims, who turned out to be proud that one of their countrymen was now a clergyman. A big crowd came. Crowther said that even though it was his mother tongue, he felt “as if I were a babe just learning to utter my mother tongue.”

Not every conversation went that well. In February 1844 he walked into a ceremony for Shango, the Yoruba god of thunder. When he rebuked the head drummer for something obscene, the man turned on him: the Christians of Freetown, he said, were the worst adulterers in town. He had been to church himself and found no good in it.

Crowther’s journal entry is startling: “To my great mortification, shame, and regret I was silenced — the charge was too true.” He didn’t argue or defend the church’s reputation. He admitted it. And when the worshippers drummed to drown him out, “the only weapons I used on this occasion were patience and an even temper.” Two of them ran after him into the street, amazed he hadn’t lost his temper.

Here is the uncomfortable lesson. Sometimes the people who criticise Christians are right. When they are, the best answer is not spin. It is honesty, and then lives that make the charge untrue. A church whose people don’t live like Christians won’t persuade anyone, however well it preaches.

One thing to do this week: think of one criticism people often make of Christians, one that is at least partly true. Instead of arguing with it, ask: is it true of me? Choose one concrete way this week to live in a way that answers it.

study_questions.question: Why did the question “Who maketh thee to differ?” fill Crowther with shame at his first sermon?
study_questions.answer: Because everything that made him stand out, his education, ordination and place in the pulpit, had been given to him. He had nothing to boast about.

study_questions.question: What did Crowther do when the Shango drummer accused Christians of immorality?
study_questions.answer: He admitted the charge was “too true” and was silenced. He answered the insults with patience and an even temper rather than anger.

study_questions.question: Why is honesty about Christians’ failures sometimes a better answer than defending them?
study_questions.answer: Because a true charge can’t be argued away, and a church that admits its faults and changes how it lives is more persuasive than one that spins them.

fields.title: The Helper of the Fatherless
fields.body_html:
“Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: The helpless committeth himself unto thee; Thou hast been the helper of the fatherless.” — Psalm 10:14 (ASV)

In the late 1830s some freed Yoruba in Sierra Leone sailed home and found that their scattered people had built a new city, Abeokuta, among huge granite rocks. Some of them were Christians, and they asked for missionaries. In August 1846, after eighteen months stuck on the coast, Crowther walked into Abeokuta.

He had been there less than three weeks when news came that he could hardly believe. His mother was alive, living with his sisters in a nearby town. He sent for her. On 21 August 1846 he wrote in his journal:

“The text for to-day in the Christian Almanac is ‘Thou art the Helper of the fatherless.’ I have never felt the force of this text more than I did this day, as I have to relate that my mother, from whom I was torn away about five-and-twenty years ago, came with my brother in quest of me. When she saw me she trembled. She could not believe her own eyes. We grasped one another, looking at one another in silence and great astonishment, while the big tears rolled down her emaciated cheeks.”

She held his hand and called him by the pet names his grandmother used to use. “We could not say much,” he wrote, “but sat still, casting many an affectionate look towards each other, a look which violence and oppression had long checked.” His two sisters, captured with him all those years ago, were alive too. “I had given up all hope, and now, after a separation of twenty-five years, without any plan or device of mine, we were brought together again.”

Her story was brutal. For much of those twenty-five years she had been a slave. By one family account she was kidnapped and sold more than once, until a daughter scraped together enough cowrie shells to buy her back. Now she was old and thin, and her son came back to her as a clergyman with a message about a God she didn’t know. At first she still worshipped the old gods, and believed her dead husband’s spirit had brought her son home. Then she fell ill, and afterwards told him: “all my hopes are in the Lord Jesus Christ, whom now I serve.” In February 1848 she was baptised, taking the name Hannah, the mother of the prophet Samuel.

When he warned her that his work would keep him travelling, she said: “You are no longer my son, but the servant of God, whose work you must attend unto without any anxiety for me.” She lived about thirty-seven more years. When she was dying in 1883, with her son far up the Niger, she told her granddaughter not to write and worry him.

Psalm 10 is not a gentle psalm. It is angry about the violent and the oppressors who drag the poor away in their nets. “Thou hast seen it,” it says to God. That is the point: God sees. He saw the raiders and the slave-dealers. He did not forget a boy torn from his mother, or the mother who lost him. And sometimes, “without any plan or device” of ours, he brings back what we thought was gone for ever.

One thing to do this week: if someone in your life is “fatherless” in any sense, alone, grieving, cut off from family, do one practical thing for them this week: a message, a meal, an invitation, your time. Be part of the way God helps the fatherless.

study_questions.question: How long had Crowther and his mother been separated, and how did they find each other?
study_questions.answer: About twenty-five years. Weeks after he arrived in Abeokuta in 1846, he heard she was alive in a nearby town and sent for her. He said it happened “without any plan or device of mine.”

study_questions.question: What did his mother say when he told her his work would keep him away?
study_questions.answer: “You are no longer my son, but the servant of God, whose work you must attend unto without any anxiety for me.”

study_questions.question: Why does it matter that Psalm 10 says “Thou hast seen it”?
study_questions.answer: Because it promises that God sees injustice and the suffering of the helpless and does not forget them, which is how Crowther understood the day his mother came back.

fields.title: In Our Own Language
fields.body_html:
“And how hear we, every man in our own language wherein we were born?” — Acts 2:8 (ASV)

When Crowther was born, Yoruba had almost never been written down. It was full of proverbs, poetry and praise-songs, all of it living in memory. By the time he died there was a Yoruba Bible, a Yoruba Prayer Book, grammars, dictionaries and schoolbooks. He wasn’t the only person behind that change, but historians call him its principal influence.

He had started collecting Yoruba words in the 1830s. His Yoruba vocabulary, published in 1843, was the first such work by a native speaker. Writing the language down was hard: Yoruba is tonal, so the same syllable on a high, middle or low pitch can mean completely different things, and it has sounds English letters can’t spell. In the 1850s a team settled a common spelling system, with marks under some letters and tone marks over vowels. The full Yoruba Bible, a team effort over forty years in which Crowther did the largest share, came out in 1884. Popular accounts sometimes say he translated it alone. He would have been the first to correct them.

Why did it matter so much? A Gambian historian, Lamin Sanneh, made the point well: when the Bible is translated into a people’s language, that language is being declared worthy to carry the word of God. Nobody has to become someone else to become a Christian. For Crowther, the gospel was not an English possession that Africans had to learn English to receive. It could speak Yoruba.

In November 1851, on a visit to England, Crowther went to Windsor Castle to talk with Prince Albert about Africa. While they bent over a map, a lady came quietly into the room. “She did not come in state,” he wrote, “but simply like any other lady.” It was Queen Victoria. When the lamp went out, the Queen lit the candles herself. Someone asked Crowther to say something in Yoruba. He gave a proverb, and then, so she could hear the language properly, the Lord’s Prayer. She said it was “soft and melodious.”

That story is often inflated into a former slave summoned before the throne. The real version is better: a quiet room, a lamp going out, and a Yoruba clergyman praying “Our Father” in his mother tongue to the Queen of England by candlelight.

There is a less comfortable side. Prince Albert, looking at the map, said Lagos “ought to be knocked down.” A month later the Royal Navy attacked Lagos to end its slave trade, and ten years later Britain annexed it. Crowther, like most African Christians of his day, saw British power as protection against the trade that had wrecked his childhood. He was right about the slave trade. He couldn’t see what colonial rule would become.

At Pentecost, the first sign of the Spirit was that people from all over the world heard God’s works “in our own language wherein we were born.” Christianity has been a translated faith from day one. God isn’t asking you to pray in a special holy dialect. He hears you in the words you actually think in.

One thing to do this week: pray this week in the language you think in, however casual. If you speak more than one language, try praying the Lord’s Prayer in your heart language, the one you grew up hearing at home, and notice whether it feels different.

study_questions.answer: Because it treats that language as worthy to carry God’s word, so people can follow Christ without first having to become someone else.

fields.title: Pressed, Not Crushed
fields.body_html:
“we are pressed on every side, yet not straitened; perplexed, yet not unto despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; smitten down, yet not destroyed” — 2 Corinthians 4:8-9 (ASV)

In 1854 Crowther went up the Niger again on a small steamer called the Pleiad, this time pushing far up its great eastern branch, the Benue. He talked with kings using everyday pictures. To a prince at Aboh, at noon with the sun blazing, he asked whether anyone would light lamps in broad daylight to help the sun shine. The sacrifices people offered to their gods, he said, were like that; Christ’s sacrifice, made once, was enough. On the hundred-and-first day he wrote that no one had died. They came home with every one of the twelve Europeans and fifty-four Africans alive. In 1841, forty-two had died. “Not unto us, but unto God, we give praise.”

In 1857 he went back to plant a permanent mission, staffed entirely by Africans. At Onitsha he left a young clergyman born to Igbo parents, John Taylor, and the interpreter Simon Jonas, with instructions that still sound wise: make friends, teach more by conversation than by sermons, learn the language, and “be not disappointed if you find the people do not act up to their engagement.”

Then, on 7 October 1857, near Jebba far up the Niger, the steamer Dayspring hit rocks and keeled over. Everyone got ashore. The ship was lost. A message went overland to the coast asking for another steamer. It took a year to come.

Fifty people camped on the riverbank. Crowther held morning and evening prayers in a tent made of mats and opened it to the sick. When a leopard raided the camp, he admitted cheerfully, “I am no gunner.” And he didn’t waste the year. He began to write down the Nupe language with a Muslim teacher and a young soldier in the Nupe army, who “felt very much interested in seeing their language being reduced to writing.” He studied Nupe farming, trade and markets. When a Fulani chief let one of his men rob a Nupe woman in front of him, Crowther told him “God would plead the cause of the oppressed” and took her to safety in the mission boat.

He lived for months as almost the only Christian in his village, among Muslims. One night he sat up late with two Muslim companions arguing about whether Christ really died on the cross. He was clear: if Christ hadn’t died, “then we are found false witnesses.” But his method was gentle. “A Mohammedan can never be brought round by his religion being quarrelled with, and abusively charged with falsehood,” he wrote, “but by kind treatment he may be led to read and study the Christian’s Bible.” When people asked him for charms, he showed them his bare arms and neck: he wore none, because “there is no help to be had from them.”

Read Paul’s list again: pressed, perplexed, pursued, smitten down. Then the “yet not” after each one. Crowther’s ship was wrecked and his plans ruined. By the end of it there was a mission at Onitsha, another upriver, the start of a Nupe grammar, and a small group of Africans who had shown they could plant churches on the Niger themselves.

When your plans get wrecked, the question isn’t whether you’re stuck on the riverbank. You are. The question is what you do with the year.

“He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, He lifteth up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, And inherit the throne of glory” — 1 Samuel 2:8 (ASV)

Henry Venn, the leader of the missionary society, believed the goal of a mission was to make itself unnecessary: plant a church, train local leaders, then step aside. His answer was obvious. The Niger should have a bishop of its own, and he should be an African. The obvious man was Samuel Crowther.

Not everyone agreed. Some European missionaries in West Africa had grave doubts about an African bishop and said so. The person who objected most strongly, though, was Crowther.

His son told this story years later, so hold it a little lightly, but it fits everything else we know. Crowther came to the committee in London in a heavy old pilot’s coat with brass buttons, and some members laughed at it. When Venn told him the plan, he said: “I am not worthy. No, sir, I am their servant in the field; I cannot accept it.” Venn sent him away for two days to think. He came back and refused again. Then Venn asked: “Samuel Adjai, my son, will you deny me my last wish asked of you before I die?” Crowther answered with old Eli’s words: “It is the Lord; let Him do what seemeth Him good.” The two men knelt together, and Venn wept.

On 29 June 1864, in Canterbury Cathedral, he was consecrated the first African bishop of the Anglican Church. According to his biographer, the naval officer who had freed him, now Admiral Sir Henry Leeke, was in the congregation. So was an elderly widow, Mrs. Weeks, who as Mrs. Davey had taught him at Bathurst. The story goes that she found her seat reserved for someone else and refused to move: “that black minister to be consecrated Bishop this morning was taught the alphabet by me.” She stayed.

One newspaper called the event a refutation of scientists who claimed Africans were mentally unfit for intellectual work. Think about that: in 1864 even Crowther’s supporters felt they had to argue that an African could think. And there were limits. He was made bishop only of lands “beyond the limits” of British territory. An African bishop over Africans was acceptable. An African bishop over Englishmen was not yet.

He asked to be addressed as “Right Reverend Bishop, and never as My Lord.” He told the committee he knew he was now “a kind of landmark” and that “any false step taken by me will be injurious to all the Native Churches.” Back in Africa, ordaining African clergy on the banks of the Niger, he wrote: “Can this be real?” In the same town, at the same time, a prince’s funeral included human sacrifices, among them a girl of eight. His title had changed. The Niger hadn’t. There was still everything to do.

Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel says God lifts the needy from the dust “to make them sit with princes.” Crowther’s mother, named after that Hannah, was still alive to see it. But notice how Crowther handled being lifted up: he didn’t want it, he didn’t grab it, and once he had it, he treated it as a weight, not a crown.

study_questions.answer: He was made bishop only of lands beyond British territory, so he had no authority over European missionaries in British colonies like Sierra Leone or Lagos.

study_questions.question: How did Crowther treat his new position once he had it?
study_questions.answer: As a responsibility rather than an honour: he refused to be called “My Lord” and knew that any false step could harm all the African churches.

fields.title: Ravens
fields.body_html:
“I hold not my life of any account as dear unto myself, so that I may accomplish my course, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.” — Acts 20:24 (ASV)

Being a bishop on the Niger meant a diocese with no roads, stretching over three hundred miles of river among a dozen peoples and languages. For years he had no boat of his own. He went up once a year in a trading steamer or a navy gunboat, and he hated what that said. People assumed he owned the ships or worked for the government. He wrote that he had to choose between being called a trader, “though I do not own a pennyworth of her,” or a warrior, “although I may not fire a blank shot.”

In September 1867 he tried his own small boat. With his son Dandeson and an English bricklayer, he stopped to visit a chief named Abokko, whom he had known for years. Abokko had fallen out with his own king and was sure Crowther owned the trading posts. He seized the boat, plundered the luggage, held them prisoner and demanded a huge ransom.

Crowther kept a diary. The first night they slept on the damp ground with nothing to eat. One of Abokko’s slaves gave him his own cloth as a blanket. A boatman gave him a robe for a pillow; he gave it to Dandeson and slept on a ridge of earth with his cap under his head. For days Abokko fed them almost nothing, and the household slaves secretly shared their own scanty food. “I often told Dandeson,” Crowther wrote, “that these slave boys and tender-feeling females were our ravens which brought us daily food as it was needed.” The man who had once been a slave was being kept alive by slaves. He promised that if he ever could, their kindness “shall not pass unrewarded.”

On Sunday he had no Bible. “I felt what it was to be deprived of the means of grace.” He and Dandeson recited Scripture from memory. Then he went to Abokko and told him this was the day God’s people everywhere met to read and pray, and he had no book. Startled, the chief had his box brought out. Abokko later sent fish that had been offered to his idol; Crowther sent it back. The ransom demand climbed to a thousand pounds, with talk of another thousand for Dandeson. Dandeson was offered the chance to leave. He refused to leave his father.

On 28 September a steamer arrived with the British vice-consul, a man named Fell. Fell decided that paying would only invite more kidnappings and urged them to run for the ship’s boat. As they pushed off, Abokko’s men fired muskets and poisoned arrows. Fell was hit by a barbed arrow and died before they reached safety.

Crowther hadn’t planned the escape; others arranged it and he went along. He wrote: “It would have been more satisfactory to me, had such been the will of God, had I been shot and my dead body taken to Lokoja instead of his.” That wasn’t a pious line. He meant it. Paul said he didn’t count his own life dear. Crowther found that easy compared with accepting that someone else had given theirs for him.

Two things to take from this. First, God’s provision often comes through the least powerful people in the room: a slave’s cloth, a shared handful of food. Second, there is Someone who did die in our place, deliberately. Crowther knew that better than anyone.

One thing to do this week: notice the “ravens” in your life this week: people with little power or status who quietly help you. Thank one of them properly, out loud or in writing. And be a raven for someone else: share something of your own with a person who is stuck.

study_questions.answer: Because, like the ravens that fed Elijah, they secretly shared their own scanty food to keep him and Dandeson alive.

study_questions.question: How did Crowther respond to Fell’s death?
study_questions.answer: He said he would rather have been shot himself and had his own body taken to Lokoja. He found it harder to accept that someone else had died for him than to risk his own life.

fields.title: Too Severe
fields.body_html:
“For it was not an enemy that reproached me; Then I could have borne it: Neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; Then I would have hid myself from him: But it was thou, a man mine equal, My companion, and my familiar friend.” — Psalm 55:12-13 (ASV)

This is the hardest chapter in Crowther’s story, and it’s easy to tell it one-sidedly in either direction. So here are the facts.

The problems were real. By the late 1870s the Niger mission stretched over three hundred miles of river. Its African staff, mostly recruited from Sierra Leone, worked far from any supervision, and the bishop could visit each station once a year at most. Many were faithful. Some were not. Worst of all, two of the mission’s African employees were convicted of treating a girl at Onitsha so cruelly that she died. One of them had been dismissed by Crowther and then, out of pity, taken back. No source suggests Crowther knew of the crime. But by common consent he was too lenient a disciplinarian. He found it hard to believe the worst of men he had trained.

He didn’t pretend all was well. He listed the agents he had suspended and dismissed. He wrote that the mission needed “decided spiritual men, because spiritual men can only teach spiritual things.” In 1884 he even offered to step aside as manager and keep working as a pioneer. The society said no. For a few years an older English secretary named James Hamilton worked alongside him, reforming the mission with firmness and without contempt. It worked.

Then a new generation arrived: young, brilliant, intensely devoted English missionaries, ready to die for Christ, and with very little patience. In August 1890, at a committee meeting at Onitsha, they and the African members “entirely failed to agree.” The English secretary, acting in the society’s name, suspended African clergy whom Crowther had ordained, in his presence. One was a veteran who had served for decades. Another was his own son, Archdeacon Dandeson Crowther. The old bishop rose to his feet to dissociate himself from what had been done and withdrew from the committee. (He was not deposed, as some retellings say. He stayed bishop until he died.)

The young men soon died or resigned, and their plans collapsed. Eight years later the society’s own historian wrote that they “were, indeed, too severe,” and “not patient enough with those who, like the venerable bishop himself, honestly differed from them.” Even then he blamed “racial weaknesses,” as if Africans as a race were weaker. That assumption, held even by kind people, was the real enemy of Crowther’s work. In 1864 the society had believed Africans could lead their own churches. By 1890 many no longer did.

How did Crowther respond? Not with the weapons used on him. The churches of the Niger Delta, led by Dandeson, stopped taking the society’s money and supported their own clergy, with the bishop’s full approval. It wasn’t a walkout from the church. It was exactly what Venn had hoped for: a church that paid its own way and ran its own affairs. Crowther accepted the society’s decisions even though he was “deeply dissatisfied” with them, and kept serving.

Psalm 55 says the worst wounds come from your own side. “It was not an enemy … Then I could have borne it.” Crowther had faced raiders, slavers and kidnappers. What nearly broke him came from fellow Christians he had blessed and sailed with. If that happens to you, and in churches it sometimes does, you can be honest that it was wrong without becoming the kind of person who did it.

One thing to do this week: if a fellow Christian has hurt you, write down plainly what happened and why it was wrong. Then write down one way you are tempted to hit back, and choose not to. If you are the one who has been too severe with someone, go and put it right.

study_questions.question: How did Crowther and the Delta churches respond?
study_questions.answer: Not by fighting back. The Delta churches began supporting their own clergy, with his approval, and stayed in the church. He accepted the society’s decisions while honestly disagreeing with them.

fields.title: Good Night
fields.body_html:
“In peace will I both lay me down and sleep; For thou, Jehovah, alone makest me dwell in safety.” — Psalm 4:8 (ASV)

In the summer of 1891, at Bonny in the Niger Delta, Crowther stood up from his desk and had a stroke. It paralysed his right hand and leg and took his voice for days. He went to Lagos to recover at the home of his daughter Abigail. “I am thankful to say that I am improving,” he wrote, wanting “to spend the remainder of my days in the service of our Divine Master.” A visitor found him sitting for hours, looking out over the sea. The society’s own historian admitted that his death was “certainly hastened by anxiety and disappointment.”

He kept working. On Christmas morning he walked to church. In the last days of December he leaned on an old friend’s arm to bless seven new schoolmasters, “tenderly, fatherly, with slow and faltering speech.” After he died, a draft letter to the society was found in his diary, in a shaky hand, never sent. He didn’t defend himself or accuse anyone. He wrote: “Though I am single-handed, I like to be improved by the ideas of others.”

On 31 December he sat at his table with his Prayer Book and hymn book as usual, then had another stroke. That night Abigail gave him his medicine at midnight. “I said, ‘Good night, father,’ and he said, ‘Good night.’” Half an hour later he was gone. The boy who had lain awake in chains the night before he was marched to market lay down at last in peace.

For a while it looked as if his work had failed. The bishop who succeeded him was an Englishman, and for decades the African bishops on the Niger served only as assistants. The mission’s staff collapsed. Even the society’s historian wrote that perhaps the Master would say, “The Mission is not dead, but sleepeth.”

It wasn’t dead. There was the Yoruba Bible. There was the beginning of written Igbo and Nupe. There were the self-supporting churches of the Delta. His grandson, Herbert Macaulay, became one of the fathers of Nigerian nationalism. And today Nigeria has one of the largest Christian populations in the world, its Anglican church among the largest anywhere, led, as Crowther always believed it should be, by Africans. In 2014, a hundred and fifty years after his consecration, the Archbishop of Canterbury stood in the same cathedral and said that Crowther had been “betrayed and let down and undermined. It was wrong.” Crowther never asked for that apology. It was for the sake of the truth.

Jesus said a grain of wheat has to fall into the ground and die before it bears much fruit. Crowther’s work seemed to fall into the ground in 1891. The harvest came after him, and he never saw most of it. That is how it often goes. You may never see what your faithfulness grows into.

A boy torn from his home in chains spent his life making sure his people would hear the gospel in their own words. He was wronged at the end and didn’t complain. His last word was a word of trust: “Good night.”

One thing to do this week: think about how you want to be remembered by the people closest to you. Write one sentence. Then pick one small, faithful thing that fits that sentence and do it every day this week, whether or not anyone notices.

study_questions.question: What did Crowther write in his last, unsent letter?
study_questions.answer: He didn’t defend himself or blame anyone. He wrote that he had never refused the committee’s suggestions and that, “though I am single-handed, I like to be improved by the ideas of others.”

study_questions.question: Did Crowther’s work fail?
study_questions.answer: It looked that way for a time, but it lived on in the Yoruba Bible, the self-supporting Delta churches and the African clergy he trained. Today Nigeria has one of the largest Christian populations in the world.

study_questions.question: What does the grain of wheat in John 12:24 have to do with his life?
study_questions.answer: His work seemed to fall into the ground and die at his death in 1891, but it bore much fruit afterwards, most of which he never saw.

fields.body_text: “In peace will I both lay me down and sleep; For thou, Jehovah, alone makest me dwell in safety.” — Psalm 4:8 (ASV) In the summer of 1891, at Bonny in the Niger Delta, Crowther stood up from his desk and had a stroke. It paralysed his right hand and leg and took his voice for days. He went to Lagos to recover at the home of his daughter Abigail. “I am thankful to say that I am improving,” he wrote, wanting “to spend the remainder of my days in the service of our Divine Master.” A visitor found him sitting for hours, looking out over the sea. The society’s own historian admitted that his death was “certainly hastened by anxiety and disappointment.” He kept working. On Christmas morning he walked to church. In the last days of December he leaned on an old friend’s arm to bless seven new schoolmasters, “tenderly, fatherly, with slow and faltering speech.” After he died, a draft letter to the society was found in his diary, in a shaky hand, never sent. He didn’t defend himself or accuse anyone. He wrote: “Though I am single-handed, I like to be improved by the ideas of others.” On 31 December he sat at his table with his Prayer Book and hymn book as usual, then had another stroke. That night Abigail gave him his medicine at midnight. “I said, ‘Good night, father,’ and he said, ‘Good night.’” Half an hour later he was gone. The boy who had lain awake in chains the night before he was marched to market lay down at last in peace. For a while it looked as if his work had failed. The bishop who succeeded him was an Englishman, and for decades the African bishops on the Niger served only as assistants. The mission’s staff collapsed. Even the society’s historian wrote that perhaps the Master would say, “The Mission is not dead, but sleepeth.” It wasn’t dead. There was the Yoruba Bible. There was the beginning of written Igbo and Nupe. There were the self-supporting churches of the Delta. His grandson, Herbert Macaulay, became one of the fathers of Nigerian nationalism. And today Nigeria has one of the largest Christian populations in the world, its Anglican church among the largest anywhere, led, as Crowther always believed it should be, by Africans. In 2014, a hundred and fifty years after his consecration, the Archbishop of Canterbury stood in the same cathedral and said that Crowther had been “betrayed and let down and undermined. It was wrong.” Crowther never asked for that apology. It was for the sake of the truth. Jesus said a grain of wheat has to fall into the ground and die before it bears much fruit. Crowther’s work seemed to fall into the ground in 1891. The harvest came after him, and he never saw most of it. That is how it often goes. You may never see what your faithfulness grows into. A boy torn from his home in chains spent his life making sure his people would hear the gospel in their own words. He was wronged at the end and didn’t complain. His last word was a word of trust: “Good night.” One thing to do this week: think about how you want to be remembered by the people closest to you. Write one sentence. Then pick one small, faithful thing that fits that sentence and do it every day this week, whether or not anyone notices.
